findings.category: A05: Security Misconfiguration / A01: Broken Access Control
findings.title: MVC CSRF default-verb matcher reconstruction is a hand-rolled OrRequestMatcher with no explicit AND-scoping requirement for webhook negation
findings.description: Tech-spec Architecture section says: 'Custom CSRF default verb matcher reconstructed via OrRequestMatcher(antMatcher("POST", "/**"), antMatcher("PUT", "/**"), ...) since MVC CsrfFilter.DEFAULT_CSRF_MATCHER is private.' Patterns.md captures the WebFlux-side invariant explicitly: the negation of the webhook path MUST be AND-combined with DEFAULT_CSRF_MATCHER, otherwise CSRF enforcement extends to ALL HTTP verbs (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) on non-excluded paths, breaking every read-only endpoint AND, more importantly, the verb list reconstruction may silently miss PATCH or DELETE, leaving state-changing requests on those verbs unprotected against CSRF. The tech-spec lists only POST and PUT in the visible example ('antMatcher("POST", "/**"), antMatcher("PUT", "/**"), ...') without enumerating the complete set the MVC default matcher actually covers (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH). The migration risks dropping PATCH/DELETE from the CSRF-required verb list.
findings.location: tech-spec.md Architecture section — SecurityConfig description; Task 3 description
findings.impact: If verbs are missed in the reconstruction, state-changing requests via those verbs become CSRF-exempt. Example: PATCH /api/profile (if added later) would bypass CSRF and an attacker-controlled site could mutate profile data via a cross-origin form. If AND-scoping is wrong, the webhook path could either lose its CSRF carve-out (200 webhooks start failing 403) or, worse, every GET on the rest of the app could start being CSRF-checked (the documented WebFlux failure mode per patterns.md).
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit Acceptance Criterion: 'TCx: CsrfFilter request matcher is AndRequestMatcher(OrRequestMatcher(antMatcher(POST,/**), antMatcher(PUT,/**), antMatcher(DELETE,/**), antMatcher(PATCH,/**)), NegatedRequestMatcher(antMatcher(POST,/webhooks/telegram/*))) — verified by integration test that asserts (a) GET / does not trigger CSRF, (b) POST /webhooks/telegram/{p} does not trigger CSRF, (c) POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH on /api/** all trigger CSRF, (d) 403 is returned when token absent.' Reference Spring Security CsrfFilter.DEFAULT_CSRF_MATCHER source to confirm exact verb list (Spring Security 6.x: POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH).

findings.category: A02: Cryptographic Failures / A05: Security Misconfiguration
findings.title: CSRF token handler downgrade — XorServerCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler → CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler removes BREACH mitigation
findings.description: Patterns.md documents the current setup uses 'CookieServerCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() plus XorServerCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler so the SPA can read the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and echo it back as the X-XSRF-TOKEN header.' The XOR handler randomizes the token per-request to defeat BREACH-style compression-oracle attacks against the SPA-readable cookie. Tech-spec Architecture line says only 'CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()' for the servlet side. There is no mention of XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler (the servlet-stack equivalent of XorServerCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler). Spring Security 6.x ships both CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler (plain) and XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler (BREACH-resistant); the default after disabling the deferred-token behavior is the plain handler. Without explicit registration, the SPA's XSRF-TOKEN cookie will contain the raw token across all requests — exactly the precondition for BREACH.
findings.location: tech-spec.md Architecture section — SecurityConfig description; Task 3 description
findings.impact: Cross-site BREACH-style attacks against the SPA's XSRF-TOKEN cookie become feasible. An attacker that can observe ciphertext lengths (e.g., via compression-sensitive sidechannels on TLS, or via an opportunistic HTTP middlebox) can recover the CSRF token byte-by-byte. The attack is publicly documented and SPA-friendly. Spring Security 6.x explicitly recommends XOR handler for SPAs.
findings.recommendation: Tech-spec must specify 'XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler' (NOT 'CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler') in SecurityConfig, configured with .setCsrfRequestAttributeName(null) per the Spring Security 6.x reactive→servlet migration guide. Add TC item: 'XSRF-TOKEN cookie value changes between two identical GET requests' (i.e., XOR randomization is active). Update Task 3 Description: explicitly mention XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler.

findings.title: RememberMeCookieSerializer wires no cookie attributes — Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite/Path/Domain must be propagated from server.servlet.session.cookie.*
findings.description: Tech-spec says: 'RememberMeCookieSerializer extends DefaultCookieSerializer; overrides writeCookieValue(CookieValue) to read SessionAttributes.REMEMBER_ME_ATTR ... and set cookieValue.setCookieMaxAge(...)'. The reactive equivalent (RememberMeWebSessionIdResolver) explicitly read attributes 'live from serverProperties.getReactive().getSession().getCookie() via PropertyMapper.alwaysApplyingWhenNonNull()' (see patterns.md). DefaultCookieSerializer on the servlet stack does NOT auto-read server.servlet.session.cookie.* — those properties are consumed by Tomcat's session cookie auto-config, but Spring Session's CookieSerializer is configured separately and defaults to httpOnly=true, secure=false, sameSite=Lax, path='/', no domain, no max-age. Without explicit setSecure(), setHttpOnly(), setSameSite(), setCookiePath(), setDomainName(), the migration silently drops env-var overrides like SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE that production deploy may depend on.
findings.impact: Cookie attribute regression: (a) Secure flag may be off if SecureBoolean env-var was used pre-flip → cookies leak over HTTP; (b) SameSite may revert to Lax instead of None+Secure (or Strict) → CSRF posture changes; (c) custom Path/Domain (e.g. scoped to /api) widens cookie scope to '/' → token reachable from frontend SSR. Production hosting is TBD (per user-spec) but staging-smoke runbooks rely on current cookie shape.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit wiring in SecurityConfig @Bean CookieSerializer: read ServerProperties.Servlet.Session.Cookie and apply setSecure(), setUseHttpOnlyCookie() (note: HttpOnly is intentionally true on RememberMe), setSameSite(), setCookieName(), setCookiePath(), setDomainName() via PropertyMapper. Mirror the pre-flip PropertyMapper.alwaysApplyingWhenNonNull() pattern. Add an integration test asserting the response Set-Cookie header includes the configured Secure/SameSite attributes. Update Task 3 description.

findings.category: A04: Insecure Design / A06: Vulnerable Components
findings.title: WebhookPayloadSizeFilter rewrite as OncePerRequestFilter — PathPattern parity not explicitly preserved
findings.description: Patterns.md mandates: 'Use Spring's PathPattern (not hand-rolled regex) for normalization parity with SecurityConfig matchers — percent-decoding, dot-segment handling.' Also: 'getValuesAsList over getFirst for headers that can repeat (Transfer-Encoding).' Tech-spec Task 9 says only 'Rewrite WebhookPayloadSizeFilter as OncePerRequestFilter with request.getHeaders(name) Enumeration handling.' No mention is made of how path matching is preserved. Servlet HttpServletRequest.getRequestURI() returns the encoded URI; if migration uses naive String.startsWith() or hand-rolled regex, attackers can bypass the 413 size check via percent-encoded path variants (e.g., /webhooks/telegram/%2e%2e/foo) which the SecurityConfig matcher may still resolve to the webhook path. Also the Transfer-Encoding: chunked rejection (which bypasses Content-Length checks) is documented in patterns.md but not explicitly enumerated in the Task 9 description.
findings.location: tech-spec.md Architecture section — WebhookPayloadSizeFilter; Task 9 description
findings.impact: Two distinct bypasses: (1) Path normalization mismatch between the filter and SecurityConfig — attacker sends an encoded path that hits the webhook controller but skips the 413 cap, allowing huge payloads to reach the controller (memory exhaustion DoS). (2) If Transfer-Encoding: chunked rejection is dropped in the rewrite, attacker sends chunked POST with no Content-Length and arbitrarily large body — bypasses the 413 cap entirely. Both vectors directly defeat the patterns.md-documented filter contract.
findings.recommendation: Update Task 9 description to enumerate the security-invariant contract: (a) match path via Spring's PathPattern (or PathPatternRequestMatcher) for parity with SecurityConfig; (b) reject Transfer-Encoding: chunked with 413 BEFORE attempting Content-Length parse; (c) reject missing/unparseable Content-Length with 413; (d) use getHeaders(name) and check every value (chunked can appear as one of multiple values). Add a TC for the test layer: 'WebhookPayloadSizeFilterTest covers encoded-path bypass attempt, chunked-encoding rejection, and multi-value Transfer-Encoding header rejection.'

findings.title: Session fixation handling — invalidate-and-recreate semantics not explicitly preserved in SecurityConfig rewrite
findings.description: Patterns.md establishes the WebFlux session-fixation invariant: 'On successful login, invalidate the pre-auth WebSession and let the framework create a fresh one before storing SecurityContext. Spring WebFlux does not do this automatically (form-login auto-config does not apply to the reactive stack).' Tech-spec Task 6 description says only 'sessions invalidated via HttpSession.invalidate()' without explicitly stating: (a) the invalidate happens BEFORE the new SecurityContext is saved; (b) the framework's SessionFixationProtectionStrategy (default 'changeSessionId' since Servlet 3.1) is configured or explicitly disabled in favor of the manual invalidate-and-recreate. Spring Security servlet auto-config applies SessionFixationProtectionStrategy automatically — if AuthService also calls HttpSession.invalidate() manually, there's a duplicate-invalidation pathway where the session ID may rotate twice or the SecurityContext may be lost to the wrong session.
findings.impact: Two failure modes: (1) Session-fixation defense skipped — pre-auth session ID survives login, enabling classic fixation attack where attacker pre-sets victim's session cookie. (2) SecurityContext stored against wrong session ID — login appears successful (200 returned, cookie issued) but subsequent requests are 401 because SecurityContextHolder write went to a session that was just invalidated. Either failure mode breaks AC16 (session continuity test) but a passing AC16 doesn't prove the fixation case is correctly handled.
findings.recommendation: Update Task 6 description to specify exact ordering: (a) load HttpSession with request.getSession(false); (b) if non-null, call invalidate(); (c) call request.getSession(true) to create fresh session; (d) save SecurityContext via securityContextRepository.saveContext(ctx, request, response); (e) verify with explicit integration test that pre-auth JSESSIONID != post-auth JSESSIONID. Alternatively (and cleaner): rely on Spring Security's SessionFixationProtectionStrategy by configuring .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionFixation().changeSessionId()) explicitly in SecurityConfig and remove manual invalidate() calls from AuthService — but document the choice clearly.

findings.title: D4 accepts BCrypt back-pressure removal under VT — DoS via /api/auth/register and /api/auth/login storm has no documented mitigation
findings.description: Decision 4 says: 'Do not add any throttling mechanism (Semaphore, work-stealing pool) for BCrypt operations during this migration. Accept that under VT each request spawns its own VT, removing the implicit ~10×CPU cap that Schedulers.boundedElastic provided. ... Current boundedElastic cap is already weak production protection (~10×CPU is order-of-magnitude below realistic DOS protection). Not a regression.' Risk R7 echoes this. From a security posture perspective: (1) /api/auth/register is unauthenticated, has no brute-force counter (per patterns.md, brute-force keys are scoped to login), and triggers BCrypt cost-12 (~250ms CPU). An attacker can run 1000 parallel register attempts and saturate CPU. (2) /api/auth/login DOES have brute-force counters, but they DEL on success and INCR-on-failure-only — so a botnet rotating real-but-non-existent emails generates BCrypt-on-DUMMY_HASH (timing-attack defense from patterns.md) on every attempt with NO throttle until per-IP threshold (20) is reached per 900s window. (3) /api/auth/forgot-password may or may not have brute-force; patterns.md notes 'forgot-password if abuse appears' suggests it currently does not. The user-spec correctly notes 'cap ~10×CPU' was 'weak production protection' but a missing-cap is meaningfully worse than a weak-cap from an availability/cost perspective.
findings.impact: Application-layer DoS via authentication endpoints. Realistic attack: 100 attacker hosts × 100 concurrent /api/auth/register POSTs = 10000 concurrent BCrypt cost-12 operations × ~250ms CPU = 2500 CPU-seconds queued onto whatever CPUs the host has. Production hosting is TBD (per user-spec) so the attacker dynamic is unknown, but staging may already be exposed. Worth noting: this is not a regression-block, but the tech-spec accepts the risk WITHOUT proposing observability to detect it (e.g., counter on time-spent-in-BCrypt, alert if > N parallel BCrypt-active VTs).
findings.recommendation: Either (preferred): add a minimal Semaphore(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() * 2) point-fix wrapping BCrypt-encode and BCrypt-matches in AuthService — Semaphore is VT-safe per Java 21 docs, costs ~10 LOC, and closes the gap. OR (documentation-only): add a TC / Risk-register item making the gap explicit and add a Micrometer counter 'auth.bcrypt.in_flight' gauge so operators can detect saturation. Either way, add an IP-based pre-throttle on /api/auth/register (currently absent per patterns.md — only login has IP throttle).

findings.title: Token-scrubber site preservation across imperative rewrite of TelegramWebhookController.receive — high regression risk
findings.description: Patterns.md enumerates 'Token-scrubber on every webhook + worker log site' and lists exact sites: 'controller DuplicateKey WARN, controller enqueue-failure ERROR, filter 413 WARN (header values too), worker INFO/WARN/ERROR sites.' The pattern is explicit: 'Wrap every WARN/ERROR string-formatted with payload-derived input through TelegramApiClient.scrubTokens(...).' Tech-spec says the rewrite 'flatMap/switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer)/onErrorResume(DuplicateKeyException, ...)/outer-onErrorResume(ex → 500) chain collapses to imperative if/else + nested try/catch' and 'Token scrubber sites and audit events preserved.' Promising 'preserved' is not the same as enforcing it. The reactive chain made scrubber sites visible (single .doOnError/.onErrorResume per error class); the imperative if/else version risks silent omission of the scrubber call on a code path that lints clean (catch (Exception ex) { log.error("..." + ex.getMessage()); ... }). Same applies to the TelegramSender outer while + inner for rewrite per Task 8.
findings.location: tech-spec.md Architecture section — TelegramWebhookController; Task 8 + Task 9 descriptions
findings.impact: Bot token leak via logs. Telegram echoes the caller's bot token back in error descriptions; if any catch-block formats ex.getMessage() into a log line without scrubTokens(), the production log ingests the plaintext token. Same risk exists for the TelegramSender rewrite — patterns.md enumerates 7 scrubber sites on the send path alone (map4xx WARN, ok=false mapper, 5xx retry observer, 429-wait announcement, terminal failure log, overall-timeout log, transport-error log).
findings.recommendation: Add explicit TC: 'TCx: Each rewritten TelegramSender / TelegramApiClient / TelegramWebhookController / ProcessTelegramUpdateJob log site is covered by a ListAppender<ILoggingEvent> test that asserts (a) the token-shaped string is NOT present in the log message, (b) the scrubbed token marker IS present.' Patterns.md explicitly says 'ListAppender<ILoggingEvent> tests are split per log site with explicit level filtering — a single combined assertion masks which site leaked.' Bring that test discipline into Task 8 and Task 9. Add a grep-gate to Pre-deploy QA: 'grep -rn "log\.\(warn\|error\)" backend/src/main/java/com/botfunnel/{webhook,bot} | grep -v scrubTokens' returns 0 matches.

findings.title: ProjectService.requireOwned signature flip — anti-enumeration 404 mapping for malformed ObjectId not explicitly preserved
findings.description: Patterns.md establishes the anti-enumeration invariant: 'requireOwned throws AppException.notFound("Project not found") for all three cases: foreign-owned, soft-deleted, and malformed ObjectId. IllegalArgumentException from Mongo on bad hex is mapped via .onErrorMap to the same 404. Never 403 — a 403 response leaks "exists, but not yours".' The .onErrorMap mechanism exists in reactive only; under sync calls, IllegalArgumentException would propagate as a 500 via GlobalErrorHandler unless an explicit try/catch wraps the findById() call. Tech-spec Task 7 description says 'ProjectService.requireOwned(...) returns Project (not Mono<Project>); same change cascades to BotService callers' but does NOT enumerate the IllegalArgumentException → 404 mapping. Patterns.md doc-update notes (AC14) mention 'flip the ProjectService.requireOwned signature note to non-reactive' but not the error-mapping note specifically.
findings.location: tech-spec.md Task 7 description; AC14 doc-update scope
findings.impact: Cross-tenant existence leak via 500-vs-404 distinguisher. Attacker probes /api/v1/projects/notahexstring — gets 500. Attacker probes /api/v1/projects/{validHex-foreign-owned} — gets 404. The distinguisher tells the attacker which project IDs are well-formed (and therefore worth pursuing). Same mapping is documented for two-resource webhook 404 anti-enumeration; the migration risks dropping it from the sync path.
findings.recommendation: Update Task 7 description to explicitly state: 'requireOwned wraps repository call in try { ... } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { throw AppException.notFound(...) }, preserving the anti-enumeration uniform-404 invariant from patterns.md.' Add a TC: 'requireOwned returns 404 (not 500) for malformed-ObjectId path parameter — integration test in ProjectControllerIT.' Same check for BotController two-resource lookup (webhook side).

findings.title: Brute-force counter Lettuce-sync semantics — INCR + EXPIRE atomicity not preserved by default in sync path
findings.description: Patterns.md documents two brute-force counter variants: (1) login default — 'brute:fail:{email} (threshold 5) and brute:fail:ip:{ip} (threshold 20), each INCR + EXPIRE 900 on first set, DEL on success.' (2) bot-connect — 'INCR-every-attempt per user (brute:bot-connect:{userId}, threshold 10, 900s TTL, EXPIRE only when INCR returns 1, DEL on success).' The 'EXPIRE only when INCR returns 1' is critical: without it, a race window exists where two concurrent INCRs both bump the counter, but the second's EXPIRE resets the TTL — the attacker can keep the counter alive indefinitely by interleaving attempts. With Lettuce reactive, INCR.then(EXPIRE) is a two-RTT chain. With Lettuce sync, it's a literal two calls. The tech-spec doesn't enumerate that this race-sensitive pattern is preserved verbatim in the sync rewrite. Worse: a naive sync rewrite might collapse to redisTemplate.opsForValue().increment(...) followed by redisTemplate.expire(...) WITHOUT the 'only-when-counter-is-1' branch — drift from the documented pattern.
findings.impact: Brute-force throttle bypass: attacker keeps incrementing a counter past the threshold, but because EXPIRE is re-applied on every INCR (drift from the documented pattern), the TTL never reaches zero. The counter is treated as 'still in the throttle window' but the threshold is never tripped — defeats the entire brute-force mitigation. Specific to login + bot-connect endpoints.
findings.recommendation: Add a TC / explicit Task 6 + Task 7 description note: 'Brute-force INCR+EXPIRE branch must follow patterns.md exactly — call EXPIRE only when INCR returns 1 (for the bot-connect variant) or use Lua-script atomic INCR-and-conditional-EXPIRE.' Add integration test: 'INCR 10 times rapidly, observe TTL is set once (does not reset on every INCR), 11th call hits threshold.' Recommend Lua atomic via redisTemplate.execute(RedisScript) to close the race window entirely.

findings.title: Spring Session in-flight bytes-shape continuity (R5) has no automated regression test — silent auth bypass risk during cutover
findings.description: Risk R5 in user-spec: 'In-flight session bytes-shape continuity. Sериализованные SecurityContext в коллекции sessions, записанные ReactiveMongoSessionRepository ДО flip\'а, должны корректно десериализоваться MongoIndexedSessionRepository ПОСЛЕ flip\'а.' Mitigation is 'manual operator step: log into dev env via UI, refresh after flip, must remain logged in.' Tech-spec Data Models section: 'spring-session-data-mongodb servlet MongoIndexedSessionRepository writes the same document shape as the reactive ReactiveMongoSessionRepository (principal field path preserved).' This addresses the read-path but not the bytes-shape of the serialized Authentication blob. If the two repositories use different SerializingConverter / DeserializingConverter / class-loader scopes, a pre-flip session may deserialize into a partial Authentication where (e.g.) the GrantedAuthority list is empty — the user appears authenticated but with no authorities, possibly bypassing role checks that fail-open on null/empty authorities. AC16 covers session-termination by principal; it does NOT cover bytes-shape correctness of an in-flight session.
findings.location: user-spec.md Risk R5; tech-spec.md Data Models section
findings.impact: Silent auth state corruption during cutover. The most-likely failure is harmless (user gets forced re-login). The worst-likely failure is a Authorities-empty Authentication: user remains 'logged in' but with no role/authorities — if any endpoint protects with hasRole(...) and fails-open on empty authorities (Spring's default is fail-closed, but custom AccessDecisionVoter or hasPermission expressions may be different), the user gains unintended access. Even if no production users exist (per user-spec process notes), a staging session could be corrupted in a way that masks the issue until production.
findings.recommendation: Add an integration test (or a one-time migration script): pre-flip, seed the sessions collection with a serialized SecurityContext via ReactiveMongoSessionRepository (or its serializer); post-flip, load via MongoIndexedSessionRepository, assert the principal, authorities list, and SecurityContext class are all preserved byte-for-byte. If serializer drift is detected, document a forced session-flush as part of the deploy runbook (db.sessions.deleteMany({})) so no in-flight sessions survive the cutover. Add explicit step to R5 mitigation: 'on flip, drop sessions collection — accept one-time re-login as the safer alternative to ambiguous deserialization.'

findings.title: CORS configuration migration — UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource swap doesn't explicitly enumerate preserved settings
findings.description: Tech-spec mentions 'org.springframework.web.cors.UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource' as the servlet-stack replacement, but doesn't enumerate that allowed-origins, allowed-methods, allowed-headers, exposed-headers, allow-credentials, and max-age are preserved verbatim. CORS misconfiguration during migration is a known vector — typical regressions include accidentally widening allowed-origins from a hostname list to '*' (which forces allow-credentials=false), or losing the cookie-bearing 'allow-credentials: true' requirement that the SPA depends on.
findings.impact: Either (a) CORS too restrictive → SPA can't reach backend (functional break, not security), or (b) CORS too permissive → cross-origin attacker can call authenticated APIs from any origin if cookies survive (e.g., allowed-origins=* with credentials=true is disallowed by spec but accidental allowed-origin=null or wildcard subdomain entries widen attack surface).
findings.recommendation: Add a TC or explicit Task 3 note enumerating the CORS settings preserved (allowed origins list, allow-credentials=true, allowed methods, etc.) and add an integration test verifying POST cross-origin with cookie returns expected Access-Control-Allow-Origin / Access-Control-Allow-Credentials response headers.

findings.title: SecurityContextHolder thread-local mode under VT — explicit confirmation not in tech-spec
findings.description: Servlet-stack Spring Security uses ThreadLocal-based SecurityContextHolder by default (MODE_THREADLOCAL). Under virtual threads, this is safe because (a) virtual threads are never pooled — each VT has its own ThreadLocal — and (b) Spring's SecurityContextHolder.setContext() / clearContext() boundaries align with request lifecycle via FilterChain. However, if the migration accidentally uses MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL (was sometimes used for async controllers to propagate context to executor threads), there's a known leakage risk: a parent VT's SecurityContext is inherited by a child VT via InheritableThreadLocal, and if the child outlives the request, security state may leak across logical boundaries. Tech-spec mentions 'ReactiveSecurityContextHolder → SecurityContextHolder' but doesn't specify the mode. The default is MODE_THREADLOCAL — safe — but ad hoc code (e.g. SecurityContextHolderStrategy customization in a config bean) could change it.
findings.impact: Cross-request security state leakage if MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL is accidentally configured AND if any task is submitted to an executor that spawns child threads. Low-probability but high-impact if it occurs.
findings.recommendation: Add a TC: 'SecurityContextHolder.getContextHolderStrategy().getClass() returns ThreadLocalSecurityContextHolderStrategy (not InheritableThreadLocalSecurityContextHolderStrategy)' — assert in an integration test. Document explicitly in patterns.md Virtual Threads section.

findings.title: Mass-assignment DTO whitelist (`@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=true)`) not enumerated in migration scope
findings.description: Patterns.md establishes: 'Every *Request record carries @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true). ownerId/owner-bound fields are NEVER read from the request body — only from ReactiveSecurityContextHolder via currentUserId().' The migration flips currentUserId() from ReactiveSecurityContextHolder to SecurityContextHolder. If the migration accidentally widens DTO contracts (e.g., adding ownerId as a request field 'because it's easier to wire under sync'), mass-assignment defense breaks. Tech-spec doesn't explicitly call out 'DTO whitelist preserved verbatim' even though the currentUserId() change is part of the auth rewrite.
findings.impact: Mass-assignment: attacker POSTs {ownerId: '<other-user-id>', ...} and resource is created/updated under the wrong owner. Cross-tenant data write. Patterns.md notes integration tests already cover this for the reactive path; need parity for the sync path.
findings.recommendation: Add a TC: 'Every *Request record retains @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=true).' Add grep-gate to Pre-deploy QA. Add explicit note in Task 6 + Task 7 descriptions: 'currentUserId() helper is rewritten from ReactiveSecurityContextHolder to SecurityContextHolder; DTOs are NOT modified — ownerId remains derived from auth context only.' Existing mass-assignment ITs (which test hostile-body) migrate verbatim from WebTestClient to MockMvc as part of the test-migration.

findings.title: EventService collapse (D12) — fire-and-forget caller semantics — silent audit loss on EventRepository failure
findings.description: Decision 12 collapses EventService API from two methods (void logEvent(...) fire-and-forget + Mono<Event> logEventBlocking(...)) to a single sync Event logEvent(...). Patterns.md notes 'Fire-and-forget side effects ... so SMTP outages never propagate to the caller. Reuse this pattern for any non-critical side effect that must not fail the user-facing request.' Under the collapse, every caller that previously fire-and-forget'd (e.g., AuthService.login auditing) now propagates eventRepository.save() failure to the caller. Functionally OK for security (better — caller knows the audit failed). BUT: if any caller wraps the call in try { } catch { /* ignored */ } to preserve the old fire-and-forget semantic, audit events are silently dropped on Mongo write failure. Patterns.md mandates audit-write-before-status-flip for the worker; same discipline must apply for AuthService.
findings.impact: Audit gap on transient Mongo outage. Security-relevant events (login, change-password, terminate-all-sessions, register, forgot-password, etc.) may be silently dropped if a caller swallows the exception. Compliance / forensic-trail consequences.
findings.recommendation: Update Decision 12: 'Callers must NOT swallow exceptions from logEvent() — either let it propagate (best) or wrap in a documented try/catch that logs a WARN with the dropped event details (acceptable for non-critical side effects, but explicitly NOT for auth/security events).' Add a TC: 'AuthService.login propagates EventRepository.save() failure to the caller (login returns 500), it does NOT silently succeed without writing the audit event.' Document the new contract in patterns.md.
